name: Equipment
content:
Items that are martial, magical, highly specialized, or otherwise elevated above the level of Gratuiti provisions and gear (see Treasure & Keeping) are considered EQUIPMENT and must be purchased individually.

EQUIPMENT CONCEPTS

The category of Equipment encompasses a wide variety of weapons, armor and many other items, but all are defined within a shared set of Equipment concepts:

TYPE

An item's TYPE is its broadest category. Type determines which base rules apply.

  • Weapon. An item designed for combat. Weapons provide Engagement Dice, Damage Dice, or both, and are subject to the weapon rules below.

  • Armor. Protective equipment worn on the body. Armor raises a character's maximum Defense, making attacks harder to land.

  • Item. Anything that isn't a weapon or armor — tools, accessories, relics and other gear. Item rules vary widely and are defined entirely by each item's description.

SUBTYPE

An item's SUBTYPE is a finer category within its Type. For Weapons, Subtype divides items into areas of training and groups items with similar characteristics. For Armor, Subtype identifies what part of the body it's worn on.

WEAPOM SUBTYPES:

  • Melee. Close-quarters weapons for hand-to-hand fighting: swords, axes, clubs, daggers. Attacks made with Melee Weapons are considered Melee Weapon Attacks. They are the tools for those who close with their enemies and thrive in the push and pull of close combat.

  • Polearm. Long-hafted weapons that give their wielder a Reach advantage: spears, halberds, pikes. Polearms always carry a Reach value that extends the wielder's threat zone (see Combat). Attacks made with Polearms are considered Melee Weapon Attacks. They suggest military training or the practical wisdom of keeping dangerous opponents at arm's length.

  • Ranged. Projectile weapons for attacking at distance: bows, crossbows, slings, javelins. Ranged weapons don't typically provide Engagement Dice. Attacks made with Ranged Weapons are considered Ranged Weapon Attacks. They suit those who like to approach conflict from a distance.

  • Firearm. Gunpowder weapons: pistols, arquebuses, muskets. Firearms don't typically provide Engagement Dice. Each Attack requires a reload, and they carry a risk of misfire (see Special Rules For Firearms below). Attacks made with Firearms are considered Ranged Weapon Attacks. Firearms are markers of modernity and specialized access — loud, powerful, and not universally available.

  • Special. Unconventional or hybrid weapons that don't fit neatly into other categories: nets, chains, kusarigama. Special weapons vary widely in their mechanics and are often specific to certain disciplines.

ARMOR SUBTYPES:

  • Head, Arms, Chest, Legs, Feet. Each Armor piece covers one of these five body location slots. All worn pieces contribute their respective Defense bonuses to your maximum Defense. Some Armor may also contribute Successes, Engagement Successes or other effects. Wearing no Armor, lighter armor or a partial suit of armor means trading coverage for mobility, lighter Load, or lower cost.

  • Shield. A held piece of Armor. A Shield provides a Defense bonus like any Armor piece and may also contribute Successes, Engagement Successes or other effects. Holding a shield occupies one hand rather than one of the body location slots.

MAGIC OR MUNDANE

All items are either MUNDANE or MAGIC:

  • Magic. Items imbued with magical properties. A magic item's effects are defined in its description and may be passive, triggered by use, activated by spending MP (see Abilities) or a Success from a Skill Check, or triggered by other conditions. Magic items follow the same Grade and Keeping conventions as all other equipment.

  • Mundane. Non-magical equipment. The term describes origin, not importance — a Mundane item can be of any quality and thus any Keeping tier. Equipment items are always Mundane unless they are marked as Magic.

GRADE

Weapons and Armor have a GRADE. An item's Grade reflects its quality of craftsmanship and general capability. There are five Grades:

  • Light. Physically light, whether by small size or delicate make.

  • Common. Solid and reliably serviceable, often of a form that is humble in origin.

  • Martial. Purpose-built for combat or skilled use.

  • Heavy. Physically heavy, whether by large size or dense material.

  • Great. Exceptionally large and/or highly specialized.

Higher-Grade weapons tend toward larger Engagement and Damage Dice and higher-Grade armor tends toward a larger Defense bonus, but an unusual design, exotic material, or special purpose can enable an item to subvert these tendencies.

KEEPING

An item's KEEPING is its economic classification — an indicator of rarity, price and what maintaining it implies about a character's circumstances. Keeping determines the item's one-time purchase cost (see Treasure & Keeping).

Note that Grade and Keeping are separate concepts: Grade describes an item's capability; Keeping describes its rarity and price. For example, a diamond-studded cudgel might be a Common weapon of Opulent Keeping, or a crudely-wrought breastplate might be Heavy armor of Modest Keeping.

In addition to the five tiers of Keeping defined in the Keeping section, Equipment items may be of two additional Keeping tiers:

  • Rare (Cost: 5) - Ancient, hard-to-find, made from unusual materials or of exceptional quality.

  • Singular (Cost: 6) - One-of-a-kind, peerless items.

These Keeping tiers are limited to Equipment items and cannot be set as a character or Quest party's Keeping (see Treasure & Keeping).

WEIGHT

An item's WEIGHT is measured in pounds and contributes to a character's Load (see Core Stats). Carrying too much weight relative to your Endurance and BODY scores pushes you toward the Weary and Twice Weary States, applying penalties to Skill Checks.

Weight is a practical trade-off on every piece of Equipment you carry. Higher-Grade armor and larger weapons tend to weigh more, but items of the same Grade can differ in weight depending on their materials and construction.

Note that Load is measured moment-to-moment, so you can choose to drop weighty gear to reduce your Load score in a pinch.

DESCRIPTION

An Equipment item's description defines any special rules or effects it provides. Some effects are passive and always active while the item is carried, wielded or worn. Others are activated by spending MP, spending a Success from a Skill Check, or triggered by a specific condition defined in the description.

WEAPON PROPERTIES

Some weapons have one or more of the following properties:

  • Finesse. This weapon can be used with either Strength or Dexterity for the Attack Roll. The choice is made each time you attack.

  • Piercing. Attacks with this weapon inflict Injury on a feat die result of 10 or Sol 🌞, rather than just Sol 🌞 (see Combat).

  • Thrown. This weapon can be used to attack a target within its Range in addition to its normal Reach. Thrown Attacks use Dexterity rather than Strength on the attack roll. The weapon is still considered a melee weapon when it is thrown, but the attack is a ranged attack.

  • Two-Handed. This weapon requires both hands to wield.

  • Reach. This Weapon extends your melee threat zone by the listed number of feet beyond the normal Adjacent range for Melee Weapons. (see Combat).

IMPROVEMENTS & SUCCESSES

Some Equipment items may offer Improvements, which can be purchased with XP and become a permanent feature of the item, just like Ability Improvements (see Abilities). They may also offer options for Skill Check Successes and effects that are triggered by Sol 🌞 and Morte 💀.

CULTURE OF ORIGIN

Each item has a CULTURE OF ORIGIN, which has no intrinsic mechanical effect, but which is tied to its availability for purchase and represents a character's history and self expression.

SPECIAL RULES FOR FIREARMS

In the world of Renaissance, firearms represent a new, powerful and volatile technology. Firearms can be hard to find, hard to repair and dangerous to use. The following rules apply to Weapons with the Firearm Subtype:

  • Each time you make an Attack with a Firearm, you must spend a Half Action to reload the Firearm before you may make another Attack with it. You must have both hands free to reload the Firearm.

  • Any time you roll Morte 💀 on an Attack Roll for an Attack made with a Firearm, the weapon misfires. Roll Injury, and you must spend an Action to repair or reset the Firearm before you can reload it.

MARTIAL TRAINING

All weapons and armor require TRAINING to use effectively. A character who lacks training with a given item Subtype suffers a penalty:

  • Weapons: Attack Rolls made with Weapons of that Subtype are Ill-Favored.

  • Armor & Shields: The item provides only half its normal Defense bonus, rounded down.

Training with a specific item Subtype is granted by a character's Mestiere or by certain abilities (See Character Creation).

BUYING, SELLING & REPAIRING EQUIPMENT

BUYING EQUIPMENT

The one-time purchase cost of an Equipment item equals the cost, in Treasure, of its Keeping tier.

What items are actually for sale at a given time depends on where the character is located relative to the Cultures of the campaign world. Different Equipment is available in different places, reflecting local craftsmanship, trade routes, and Cultural specialties. The same kind of item made in two different places may have different mechanical traits or may only differ in style.

SELLING EQUIPMENT

Selling a piece of Equipment in good repair yields half its original cost in Treasure, rounded down. A broken piece of Equipment generally yields no Treasure when sold, though the GM may make exceptions in the case of rare materials or unusual circumstances.

BREAKING & REPAIRING EQUIPMENT

If an Equipment item becomes broken, whether through mishap or as the result of a mechanical effect, the item no longer offers any of its mechanical benefits.

Mundane items can be repaired in one of two ways:

  • A skilled craftsperson will generally repair an item for a fee of half the item's original cost.

  • To repair an item yourself, you must spend a number of hours working on it equal to its original cost in Treasure. At the end of that time, roll Craft against a Difficulty equal to five times the item's original cost in Treasure. On a pass, the item is repaired. On a failure, it remains broken.

For magic items, repair may require specialized knowledge, rare materials, or other conditions, at the GM's discretion.
